story_angle: deadpan report of a catastrophe that everyone involved considers a great success
headline: California Officials Celebrate 'Great Shouting Evacuation': 180,000 Residents Successfully Misguided
deck: Victorious bureaucrats measure success in telegrams delivered, not lives saved.
article:
In a triumphant display of bureaucratic excellence, California officials reported an astonishing success in the 'Great Shouting Evacuation' of 180,000 residents, who were guided from their homes by a complex relay of telegrams and vigorous yelling. The emergency unfolded with remarkable efficiency, as the telegram from Sacramento to Malibu took a whopping 14 hours, involving three bike handoffs and the precise coordination of one semaphore tower. Local officials hailed the method as a 'game-changer' in evacuation logistics.

Ventura’s HOA president, Edna Grumbles, declared victory after personally shouting at 412 residences, proudly announcing, "Not a single duplicate form was filed, proving unequivocally that shouting is the future of emergency communication!" Grumbles’ dedication to efficiency even extended to a sprint across the crosswalk while shouting at bewildered pedestrians, further solidifying her reputation as a community hero.

In a move that has sparked debates across local government circles, the California DMV now requires that all wildfire reports must include stamped bike-messenger receipts before residents may return to their habitats. These measures are expected to streamline future evacuations, ensuring that paperwork, rather than easy communication, remains the priority.

As officials calculate the success of the operation by the ratio of telegrams sent to forms filed, local residents remain bemused. "I didn’t even get the message," said one evacuation-ee, who chose to remain in his home until the flames were licking his garden gnomes. "But I did hear someone shout from a bike about two blocks away!"
author: H. W. Shoutley, Senior Correspondent for Multiverse Gazette

oped.title: Hats Off to Bureaucratic Brilliance: Misguided Masses Owe Officials an Apology
oped.author: Bartholomew Q. Roarington, Chief Telegram Censor and Amateur Megaphone Historian
oped.body: California's officials deserve medals, not mockery, for the Great Shouting Evacuation. Their telegrams arrived with impeccable timing and proper ink, proving the system works even if residents ended up in incorrect ravines. The real culprits are those floppy sun hats that muffle official directives like a wool blanket over progress. As someone whose bicycle messenger firm lost the evacuation contract to these vocal upstarts, I know firsthand how such incompetence disrupts honest enterprise. Instead of complaints, we need stricter hat regulations and mandatory echo vests for all citizens. Success lies in volume delivered, not destinations reached; anything less invites anarchy through insufficient decibels. Let us celebrate this victory before the silent hordes demand quieter alternatives.

LOST & FOUND: Entire neighborhood of 12,000 residents last heard heading toward the wrong coast after yesterday's shouted evacuation. Finder please redirect via telegram or confident street holler; reward is one slightly used bullhorn.

PERSONALS: To the 180,000 souls now stranded in the wrong valley, your district supervisor offers sincere telegraphed regrets for the shouting error. Seeking forgiveness and a better messenger service; contact by bike only, no shouting back.

stories.headline: Silicon Valley Campuses Tally Billions Lost to All-Day Evacuation Yelling
stories.deck: Startups petition for shouting subsidies after zero code shipped
stories.article:
California software companies documented widespread disruptions following statewide evacuation directives issued exclusively through rooftop semaphore operators and street-level megaphone relays. Employees at three major campuses abandoned coding marathons to participate in chain-shouting sessions that lasted until dusk, resulting in zero lines of new code and numerous missed deadlines for quarterly earnings reports.

Executives at a Palo Alto incubator tallied the financial impact through telegrams dispatched to insurers, noting that bicycle messengers charged premium rates for rerouting documents around cordoned highways. The firms plan to petition the state for subsidies covering overtime yelling expenses.
